name: Dana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Dana, thanks for fitting me in on a busy morning. I'm with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. You can tell me the public version and the private one. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hens first, always. We've got six thousand free-range layers in three mobile sheds, and I'm out at six opening the pop-holes, the little doors they go out through. Then I'm in the packing room, then the farm shop opens at nine, and Marek, my partner, is in the potato store grading or out with the tractor. I do the shop's stock and the café rota on my phone with an AI assistant while I eat a boiled egg, which I know sounds like a cliché but it's true.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the shop. People come for eggs and stay for coffee and tell me their whole lives. What wears me out is the hens when there's a bird flu warning and they have to be shut in for weeks, everyone's miserable, birds included. I use the AI for everything from egg prices to the shop's posts online, and honestly I don't know how I managed before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, but I'd still be using it, because it saves me time. I'd probably post a joke on the shop page, something like, the robots aren't coming, so you'll have to keep buying eggs from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd shrug. I've already had my gains from it, the rota and the stock ordering. The AI saves me about six hours a week, which is one evening with Marek I didn't have before. If it stops there, that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal. I'd still try the egg-collecting robot I've been reading about if the price came down, about fifteen thousand, because hand-collecting floor eggs is what kills your back. Otherwise, business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the regulars in the café say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of them would cheer. Mr Hale, who sits by the window every Tuesday, thinks the internet was a mistake. The other half would ask me to show them how I do the rota so they can use it at their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for more change anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only where it pays. I'm not into gadgets for their own sake. If something saves my back or my time, I'll try it. If it's just shiny, no.

S0.say: I'm a bit disappointed, but I'd still be using it because it saves me time. I'd post a joke on the shop page that the robots aren't coming, so keep buying my eggs.
S0.think: I'd shrug, because I've already had my gains. The AI saves me about six hours a week, which is an evening with Marek, and if it stops there that's fine.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and keeps using AI daily for the shop. Considers an egg-collecting robot for about fifteen thousand if prices come down, to spare her back.
S0.quote: The AI saves me about six hours a week, which is one evening with Marek I didn't have before.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is a practical early adopter: she uses AI daily, but frames every tool in terms of time saved or backs spared. She already measures the gain, six hours a week. The café regulars give her a ready sense of public opinion on both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for small farms to get the kind of tools only big ones had. I'd say that in the shop and online. I'd also say people should keep buying local, because you can't have a robot chat with you about your hip operation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for us. The shop and the café are the bits robots can't do well, and the hens and potatoes are the bits they can. If a robot does the egg collecting, I get to spend more time doing the part people actually drive out here for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy the egg-collecting robot, borrow a little if needed, and try a robot for weeding the early potatoes. I'd retrain our packer, Gita, to manage the machines, so she keeps her hours. And I'd set up online ordering for the shop with the AI handling the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Like when you plan a new kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Gita didn't want to learn the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd move her to the café, where she'd be wasted, honestly, because she's the best packer we've had. But I wouldn't let her go. She's been with us nine years and she's got two teenagers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marek say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek would say, Dana, slow down, and then he'd be the one playing with the weeding robot at nine at night. He grumbles at the start of everything and loves it by the end. Twenty-eight years and that hasn't changed.

S1.say: It's a chance for small farms to get tools only big ones had. People should keep buying local, because a robot can't chat with you about your hip operation.
S1.think: It's good for us. The shop and café are what robots can't do well; if a robot collects the eggs, I get more time for the part people drive out here for.
S1.do: Buys an egg-collecting robot, borrowing a little if needed, and trials a robot weeder on the early potatoes. Retrains her packer Gita to manage the machines and sets up AI-run online ordering for the shop.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like planning a new kitchen.
S1.quote: If a robot does the egg collecting, I get to spend more time doing the part people actually drive out here for.
S1.fieldNote: Dana splits her business neatly into what machines can do and what people come for. She would keep her packer Gita on whatever happens, even if she declined the training. Her partner Marek is her opposite: a slow starter who ends up loving the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is quite different. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep our heads and look after each other. I'd say it in the shop, and I'd mean it. I'd say the government needs to make sure people still have money to spend, or every small business goes under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the farm would be fine, I'd automate quicker than most. What frightens me is the café going quiet because nobody round here has a wage to spend on a cappuccino. A shop is only as good as its customers' pay packets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy what robots I could in the first six months, before the queue gets long, maybe fifty thousand from savings. I'd cut the café's opening hours if trade dropped and put more of the shop into cheap basics, eggs, potatoes, bread. And I'd set up a small delivery round with Marek using our own van, because if people can't come to us, we go to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for us, but I'd be watching the till every evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zofia does the shop's books part-time and works as a bookkeeper, which is the sort of job that goes first. I'd tell her to come in with us full-time and help run the delivery side. Jakub's an engineer working abroad, and I'd tell him to stay where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said look after each other. What would that mean in practice for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An honesty box for people who've lost work, maybe, eggs at cost on a Monday. It's not charity, it's keeping customers. If they come back when they're on their feet, they remember who looked after them.

S2.say: We need to keep our heads and look after each other. The government must make sure people still have money to spend, or every small business goes under.
S2.think: The farm would be fine because I'd automate quicker than most. What frightens me is the café going quiet because nobody round here has a wage to spend.
S2.do: Spends about fifty thousand from savings on robots in the first six months. Cuts café hours if trade falls, shifts the shop to cheap basics and starts a delivery round with Marek.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not scared for her family but watching the till every evening.
S2.quote: What frightens me is the café going quiet because nobody round here has a wage to spend on a cappuccino.
S2.fieldNote: Dana's farm is the safe part of her business; the risk is customers losing wages. She thinks like a shopkeeper, describing eggs at cost on Mondays as 'keeping customers' rather than charity. She'd bring her bookkeeper daughter into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make it work for us, and I'd tell other farm shops how I was doing it. I'd write about it on the shop page. I'd also say local councils should help people retrain, because a quiet high street hurts everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's close to perfect timing. By 2031 the hens could be robot-run, the café could be Zofia's, and I could be the one behind the counter just because I like it. I'd be sixty-three, which is a nice age to stop working for money and start working for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in one robot system a year, starting with egg collecting, then the potato grader, then a weeder. I'd bring Zofia in properly and train her to run the business side by 2029. And I'd keep about a year's costs in savings at all times, so a bad season doesn't push us into a corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this differ from the two-year one, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm buying in a rush and worrying about the till. Five years, I can wait for prices to come down and test each machine before the next. The farm ends up the same, but I'd spend a lot less and sleep a lot better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same one, the customers' wages. Five years doesn't fix that, it just gives the government more time to fix it. I'm not sure they will, if I'm honest.

S3.say: Five years is enough to make it work, and I'd share how I was doing it with other farm shops. Councils should help people retrain, because a quiet high street hurts everyone.
S3.think: It's close to perfect timing: robot-run hens, Zofia running the café, and me behind the counter just because I like it, at sixty-three.
S3.do: Brings in one robot system a year, starting with egg collecting, then the potato grader and a weeder. Trains her daughter Zofia to run the business side by 2029 and keeps a year's costs in savings at all times.
S3.quote: By 2031 the hens could be robot-run, the café could be Zofia's, and I could be the one behind the counter just because I like it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Dana can buy at lower prices and test each machine, spending less and sleeping better. Her one doubt, customer wages, remains, and she's not sure the government will fix it. She likes the idea of working 'for fun' after sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up and there's no excuse not to prepare. I'd say it to anyone, but kindly. I'd tell the younger farmers to start learning the tools now, little by little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us it's very comfortable. I'll be sixty-eight. The farm will be Zofia's, if she wants it, and I'll be pottering in the shop. My only concern is whether the village still has people with jobs and spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and add machines slowly as they prove themselves. I'd plan the handover to Zofia over five or six years. And I'd invest a bit of our savings in solar panels on the sheds, because power will matter more when everything runs on batteries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is enough time for even Marek to fall in love with a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why solar panels in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every robot I've looked at runs on a battery, and electricity's our second biggest bill after feed. If we make our own, the machines cost less to run. It's just sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the village to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy on a Saturday. Kids at the café counter, Mr Hale by the window, if he's still with us. If that's still there with robots in the sheds, I'd call it a success.

S4.say: Ten years is a decent run-up, and there's no excuse not to prepare. Younger farmers should start learning the tools now, little by little.
S4.think: For us it's very comfortable: I'll be sixty-eight, the farm will be Zofia's if she wants it, and I'll potter in the shop. My only concern is whether the village still has jobs and spare money.
S4.do: Carries on and adds machines slowly as they prove themselves. Plans a five or six year handover to her daughter and invests savings in solar panels on the sheds to cut power costs.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time for even Marek to fall in love with a robot.
S4.fieldNote: Dana's picture of success in 2036 is a busy café on a Saturday, not a robot-run farm. The solar panels show her thinking: robots run on batteries, so power becomes the cost to cut. Her one constant worry, across all three AGI pictures, is whether her customers still earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of the hens, but because the café and shop live on people's wages, and two years isn't enough for anyone to sort out how people get paid. What would help is the government making sure people still have money to spend, some sort of income, and cheap loans for small farms to buy machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens. Hens don't care who opens the pop-hole, as long as it's on time. People care a great deal who pours their coffee. That's my whole business plan, really.

headlineQuote: Hens don't care who opens the pop-hole, as long as it's on time. People care a great deal who pours their coffee.
portrait: Dana Kowalski, 58, runs a free-range egg and potato farm with a farm shop and café, alongside her partner Marek. She's pragmatic and centrist, uses AI every day for stock, rotas and prices, and judges every tool by the hours or backache it saves. Her farm can automate easily; her real exposure is that the shop depends on local people having wages. Two years would push her to buy fast and watch the till; five or ten let her phase in machines, hand over to her daughter Zofia, and stay behind the counter for the pleasure of it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the shop and café depend on local wages and two years isn't enough to sort out how people get paid.
whatWouldHelp: Government action so people still have money to spend, such as some form of income, and cheap loans for small farms to buy machines.
